subject: human teeth
title: What If You Never Brushed Your Teeth Again? A Timeline

scenes.text: What if you never brushed your teeth again? Day one is already the problem.
Within minutes of eating, bacteria feast on the leftovers. After one full day, they've laid down a thick film of plaque.
Within about 48 hours to a week, that plaque hardens into yellow tartar. No brush removes it now, only a dentist's tools.
After a month, your gums fight back: red, swollen, bleeding when you eat. That's gingivitis.
By a year, it becomes periodontitis. Gums pull away, the bone underneath breaks down, and teeth loosen and fall out.
Your mouth hosts about 700 species of microbes. Let them into bleeding gums and research links them to clogged arteries and heart disease. Two minutes, twice a day.

description:
What if you stopped brushing your teeth for good? Plaque forms within a day, hardens into tartar within roughly 48 hours to a week, gingivitis sets in after about a month, and within a year it can become periodontitis, with bone loss and loose teeth.
Timelines vary with genetics, diet and health, but the sequence is well established: tartar can only be removed professionally, and the mouth's roughly 700 microbial species have been linked by researchers to cardiovascular disease when gum infection lets them into the bloodstream. The American Dental Association's advice is two minutes, twice a day, with fluoride toothpaste.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Tartar in two days, gingivitis in a month, loose teeth in a year. What is the longest you have ever gone without brushing? Drop your own what-if below.
